strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: geometry compression across heterogeneous point clouds with one shared pretrained model. Combining spatial and occupancy-channel context with lightweight instance adaptation is technically plausible and relevant to practical 3D data storage.

Table 1 provides unusually broad evaluation across 15 datasets, including five designated OOD datasets. Ours-U reports a 10.75% average bitrate reduction relative to G-PCC v23, with particularly strong results on VGGT and the three synthetic corruption datasets. These results support the usefulness of the unified approach even though it does not win every comparison.

The lossless coding procedure explicitly transmits quantized adapted weights and uses those same weights for geometry encoding and decoding. Table 4 accounts for this overhead: on GS, the total decreases from 13.307 to 11.743 bpp, including 0.319 bpp for weights. This is meaningful evidence that adaptation can yield net savings.

The ablations provide evidence for combining the context components: Table 2 reports a 9.88% reduction for the full model versus 7.74% with spatial convolution and spatial grouping alone, at nearly identical parameter counts. Feature caching also offers a sensible way to make head-only adaptation computationally manageable.
weaknesses: The central generalization claim is not adequately isolated from training-data and adaptation advantages. Ours-U uses a diverse mixed training corpus, while Section 4.2 states that KITTI-trained models are used for OOD evaluation. Results for competing methods trained on unified data are deferred to an appendix absent from the supplied manuscript. Consequently, the main comparison cannot establish how much improvement comes from the proposed architecture rather than broader training exposure.

The evidence for IAFT as the mechanism addressing OOD data is incomplete. Table 1 enables adaptation for all medium and hard datasets, but does not provide corresponding fixed-model results for each dataset. Table 3 does not identify its evaluation set, and Table 4 examines GS, which Table 1 labels in-distribution. The manuscript therefore demonstrates that adaptation can help, but does not directly establish its claimed contribution across the five OOD datasets.

Essential reproducibility details are missing. The supplied PDF contains no appendix despite repeatedly referring to it for benchmark construction, training mixtures, additional comparisons, theoretical proofs, and the lossy algorithm. Dataset sizes and splits, voxelization precision, corruption strengths, training schedules, adaptation hyperparameters, and weight-quantization settings are not adequately specified. These omissions affect interpretation of both the benchmark and the reported bitrates.

Originality is primarily in the combination and application of existing ideas, and the distinctions need stronger substantiation. Checkerboard spatial/channel context and parameter-efficient instance adaptation already appear in the cited literature. The particularly relevant space-to-channel point-cloud method [28] receives no substantive comparison. The claimed occupancy/voxel equivalence also concerns representational information and receptive-field coverage; without the referenced proofs, it does not establish equivalent convolutional expressiveness or better compression.

The lossy extension is underspecified: transmitting a point count and selecting likely occupied locations does not explain how the sequential spatial/channel dependencies are handled during reconstruction. Figure 5 provides encouraging curves, but the PSNR definition, reconstruction settings, and quantitative aggregate rate-distortion comparisons are absent. Its caption calls excluded baselines incompatible, whereas Section 4.3 attributes their exclusion to suboptimal performance.

Several claims exceed the evidence. The 13-dataset winning count combines specialized and unified variants; it is not the performance of the single universal model alone. The lossless percentage reductions are incorrectly called BD-Rate savings, and the parameter table totals seven models for Ours while apparently reporting individual baseline model sizes. These are correctable reporting issues, but they weaken the presentation of universality and deployment efficiency. Overall, the credible empirical gains place the paper near acceptance, while unresolved comparison controls and missing methodological details keep the recommendation borderline.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: deploying one geometry codec across diverse point-cloud distributions. Combining spatial/channel occupancy context with lightweight instance adaptation is technically coherent and practically relevant.

Table 1 provides substantial empirical evidence across 15 datasets. The unified model achieves a 10.75% average bitrate reduction against G-PCC, and the specialized/unified variants collectively obtain the best results on 13 datasets. These are meaningful results despite exceptions to the superiority claims.
Table 2 supports the combined context design: the full model improves bitrate by 9.88% over its baseline, versus 7.74% without channel grouping at nearly identical parameter counts.

The adaptation experiment explicitly accounts for transmitted weights. On GS, Table 4 reduces total bitrate from 13.307 to 11.743 bpp, including 0.319 bpp of model overhead. Caching frozen features is a sensible way to reduce adaptation cost.
weaknesses: The central generalization claim is not adequately isolated. Ours-U combines mixed-data training with adaptation on medium/hard samples, while Section 4.2 states that KITTI-trained models are used for OOD evaluation. Matched mixed-training baselines are deferred to an unavailable appendix. The supplied results therefore do not establish how much improvement comes from the proposed architecture, broader training data, or test-instance optimization.

Reproducibility has material gaps. The supplied PDF contains no appendix, although essential dataset definitions, splits, corruption settings, theoretical proofs, and codec details are repeatedly deferred there. Training schedules, IAFT optimization settings, and weight-quantization settings are also insufficiently specified. In particular, the construction of Dense/Sparse and the separation of synthetic test samples from training data cannot be verified.

The lossy extension is underspecified. Section 3.4 does not explain sufficiently how selecting the k most probable occupied locations interacts with sequential spatial/channel conditioning, or how subsequent contexts are constructed from reconstructed geometry. Figure 5 supplies curves but cannot substitute for a reproducible decoding procedure.

The originality is primarily an integration of established ideas. Checkerboard space-channel context models and parameter-efficient instance adaptation are acknowledged in related work, but their distinction from this design is argued more strongly than demonstrated. The occupancy-specific implementation has value, yet the claims of pioneering a new compression paradigm exceed the evidence.

The ablations leave important attribution questions open. Table 2 does not identify its evaluation dataset or provide an SC-only configuration, despite claiming an individual SC benefit. Table 3 uses 800 adaptation iterations whereas the principal benchmark uses 200; dataset-wise adaptation gains and overhead under the main setting are not provided.

Presentation overstates some findings: Ours-U does not consistently outperform existing methods, including on MVUB, GS, and S3DIS; lossless percentage bitrate reductions are incorrectly called BD-rate savings. Overall, the broad measured gains and useful design place the paper near acceptance, but the unresolved comparison controls and missing operational details keep the recommendation borderline.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: deploying one geometry codec across dense, sparse, and unfamiliar point clouds. The shared multiscale architecture and lightweight instance adaptation form a coherent, practically motivated contribution.

Table 1 provides substantial empirical support across 15 datasets. Ours-U reports 10.75% average bitrate savings over G-PCC, and the specialized and unified variants collectively achieve the best results on 13 datasets. The unified model also outperforms the specialized variant on all five designated OOD datasets.

The adaptation mechanism is technically plausible and explicitly accounts for transmitted weights. On GS, Table 4 reduces the total rate from 13.307 to 11.743 bpp, including 0.319 bpp of weight overhead. Caching frozen features makes prediction-head adaptation computationally attractive.

The ablations support combining spatial and channel context: the complete model achieves a 9.88% reduction against the ablation baseline, compared with 7.74% without channel grouping at nearly identical parameter counts. Reported decoding time remains 0.46 seconds with adaptation.
weaknesses: The central generalization claim is not sufficiently isolated from training-data and adaptation advantages. Ours-U uses mixed-data training, while the OOD comparisons use KITTI-trained baselines; medium and hard samples additionally receive IAFT. Comparisons with jointly trained RENO-U and SparsePCGC-U are deferred to an appendix absent from the supplied manuscript. The available results demonstrate the complete system's effectiveness, but do not establish how much comes from UCM, broader training, or adaptation.

Essential reproducibility information is missing: dataset splits and per-dataset sample counts, coordinate quantization, definitions of Dense/Sparse, corruption severities, training schedules and mixture ratios, and IAFT learning rate, regularization strength, and weight-quantization settings. The supplied PDF contains eight main pages and references, without the repeatedly cited appendix. These omissions materially limit verification of the benchmark and OOD designation.

Adaptation evidence is concentrated in an aggregate ablation and the GS example, which is marked in-distribution. There is no per-OOD-dataset comparison of the same universal checkpoint with and without IAFT. Table 3 uses 800 iterations whereas the main benchmark uses 200, leaving the main operating point's incremental rate benefit and weight overhead insufficiently characterized.

Originality is primarily in the combination and geometric implementation of existing ideas. Checkerboard and channel grouping, instance-adaptive compression, and parameter-efficient adaptation are acknowledged precedents. The strong claims of pioneering a new paradigm exceed the demonstrated distinction, particularly without a closer comparison to the cited space-to-channel point-cloud method and lossless instance-adaptive work.

The lossy extension is underspecified: Section 3.4 does not adequately explain reconstruction and causal context updates when occupancy symbols are inferred rather than transmitted. Figure 5 also shows that Ours-U is substantially weaker on ScanNet than several alternatives. Calling the lossless table's savings 'BD-Rate' is a separate, readily correctable reporting error.

strengths: The lossless compression contribution supports a weak acceptance. Combining spatial grouping at the occupancy-code scale with channel grouping yields a practical codec for heterogeneous point clouds. Table 1 reports average bitrate reductions of 11.93% for specialized models and 10.75% for the universal model relative to G-PCC v23.

The evidence extends beyond aggregate benchmark results. Table 7 compares models trained on the same mixed dataset without instance adaptation, showing that the proposed context model itself is competitive, particularly on LiDAR data. Tables 2 and 10 further examine architectural components and alternative grouping configurations.

Instance-adaptive tuning has a convincing practical implementation: caching frozen features makes prediction-head optimization inexpensive, and transmitted weights are included in the bitrate. On GS, Table 3 reports an entropy-coding reduction of 1.883 bpp against 0.319 bpp of weight overhead. Figures 9–11 investigate iteration count, tunable modules, quantization, and weight coding.

The benchmark covers a useful range of dense objects, LiDAR, reconstructed scenes, Gaussian-splat coordinates, and synthetic corruptions. The supplement provides substantial implementation detail, including training splits, quantization settings, sampling weights, architecture, and optimization hyperparameters. These are meaningful contributions to evaluating compression beyond familiar datasets.
weaknesses: The strongest OOD comparison does not isolate architecture from training diversity and adaptation. Section 4.2 uses KITTI-trained competing models for OOD evaluation, whereas Ours-U benefits from mixed training and IAFT. The matched mixed-training comparisons in Table 7 cover only the seven easy datasets. Consequently, the reported OOD advantages are useful system-level results, but do not establish how much competing universal models would improve under equivalent training and adaptation.

The lossy BD-rate evidence needs more rigorous reporting. Table 9 reports approximately 91% average savings over G-PCC on dense datasets, but Figure 5 shows little or no visible PSNR overlap between their displayed curves on several human datasets. The integration intervals and any extrapolation are unspecified, so these large savings cannot be verified as standard overlapping-range BD-rate comparisons. The PSNR formulation and baseline codec configurations also need clearer specification.

The lossy extension is less completely specified than the lossless codec. Table 4 switches to a single-stage, 256-output model, and Table 9 increases universal-model parameters from 9.77M to 14.92M; this qualifies the claim that the same model seamlessly handles both modes. Moreover, Equations 22–24 select k code locations and then predict multi-bit occupancy codes, which does not by itself ensure k reconstructed child points. The relationship between the transmitted count, selected locations, and expanded geometry, together with training of the lossy path, remains unclear.

Originality is primarily in the integration and adaptation of existing ideas. Checkerboard/spatial-channel contexts and parameter-efficient instance adaptation have precedents acknowledged in the paper. Theorem 1 establishes a straightforward bijection, while Theorem 2 establishes a maximum geometric span rather than a general equivalence of effective sparse-convolution receptive fields or a guarantee of sparsity robustness. The empirical contribution is stronger than the theoretical and 'first' claims suggest.

Some deployment and reproducibility claims exceed the supplied evidence. Section 9.4 calls 2.84 seconds an extreme upper bound, although longer tuning configurations are explicitly evaluated, and 0.28 seconds per KITTI frame does not establish stringent real-time suitability. Synthetic corruption parameters and exact source-instance lists are incompletely specified, while Section 8.2's OOD dataset list conflicts with Table 6. These issues limit reproducibility and interpretation, but do not overturn the supported lossless compression results.

strengths: The lossless compression contribution supports weak acceptance. AnyPcc combines occupancy-code spatial context, channel conditioning, and lightweight instance adaptation into a useful codec. Its practical contribution is supported even though some universality and novelty claims are overstated.

The evaluation covers substantially different geometries across 15 datasets, including dense objects, LiDAR, reconstruction outputs, and synthetic corruptions. Table 1 reports average bitrate reductions over G-PCC v23 of 11.93% for specialized models and 10.75% for the universal model, with competitive results across most datasets.

The supplementary evaluation strengthens the evidence beyond the main comparisons. Table 7 retrains RENO and SparsePCGC on the mixed training corpus and evaluates AnyPcc without adaptation, demonstrating that the base architecture provides benefits independently of instance fine-tuning.

Adaptation overhead is explicitly included. On GS, Table 3 reports a geometry-rate reduction from 13.307 to 11.424 bpp with a 0.319 bpp weight payload, establishing a substantial net saving. The iteration, adapted-module, quantization, and weight-coder experiments further substantiate this design.

The ablations examine spatial grouping, channel grouping, convolution, model width, and training mixture. Architectural diagrams, training hyperparameters, dataset splits, and preprocessing details provide a substantial foundation for reproduction.
weaknesses: The strongest OOD comparison does not fully separate architecture, training diversity, and adaptation. Section 4.2 uses KITTI-trained specialized models for OOD evaluation, whereas Ours-U benefits from mixed-data training and IAFT. The matched universal baselines in Table 7 cover only seven standard datasets, excluding the OOD cases central to the motivation. This limits attribution of the reported generalization advantage.

The lossy method has a consequential specification ambiguity. Equations 22–24 select k occupied code locations and assign each a nonzero occupancy code; expanding those codes produces a number of child points determined by their population counts, not necessarily k. The claimed preservation of the ground-truth point count therefore does not follow without a clearer scale convention or additional selection procedure. Moreover, Table 4 switches to a separate single-stage lossy model, and parameter count increases from 9.77M to 14.92M, qualifying the claim of one unchanged model for both modes.

Novelty is primarily in the particular integration and application. Channel grouping, spatial grouping, and parameter-efficient instance adaptation have acknowledged precedents. Theorem 1 establishes a representation bijection; Theorem 2 establishes a maximum geometric span, rather than equivalence of effective sparse-convolution connectivity or guaranteed robustness. These results do not justify the stronger theoretical and pioneering language.

Claims of universal superiority exceed the evidence: Table 1 shows losses on GS and S3DIS, and the universal model trails specialized alternatives on several standard datasets. Lossy evaluation excludes seven datasets because baseline rate points were unstable; lossless trends cannot establish the missing rate-distortion results.

Several reproducibility and deployment claims need qualification. Synthetic corruption formulas omit concrete parameter settings and seeds, and Section 8.2's OOD list conflicts with Table 6. Section 9.4 calls 2.84 seconds an extreme upper bound without reporting dataset-specific worst-case latency or peak memory, particularly relevant to the 47-million-point S3DIS sample. Its claims of stringent real-time suitability and seamless standards compatibility are not demonstrated.

strengths: The paper makes a useful contribution to point cloud geometry compression: a shared context model combines spatial grouping of occupancy codes with channel grouping, while cached prediction-head adaptation provides an adjustable compression–encoding-time trade-off. The lossless formulation is coherent, and the architecture is described in substantial detail.

The lossless evaluation is unusually broad, covering 15 datasets with dense objects, LiDAR, reconstructed geometry, and synthetic corruptions. Table 1 reports average bitrate reductions of 10.75% for the unified model and 11.93% for specialized models relative to G-PCC v23. The unified model achieves competitive compression without maintaining separate pretrained models for each category.

The supplementary experiments strengthen attribution of the gains. Table 7 retrains RENO and SparsePCGC on the same mixed corpus and compares them without IAFT; AnyPcc-U remains competitive on dense data and substantially stronger on KITTI and Ford. Tables 2 and 10 systematically examine context grouping, supporting the proposed architectural combination.

IAFT evaluation explicitly accounts for transmitted weights. On GS, Table 3 shows geometry bitrate decreasing from 13.307 to 11.424 bpp with a 0.319-bpp weight payload, demonstrating a meaningful net benefit. Iteration, module-selection, quantization, and weight-coder studies further substantiate the practical design. Together, these results provide a stronger case for acceptance than the remaining limitations provide for rejection.
weaknesses: The central OOD comparison does not fully separate architectural generalization from training diversity and test-time adaptation. Section 4.2 uses KITTI-trained baseline models for OOD evaluation, whereas Ours-U benefits from mixed-data training and IAFT. The matched unified-training comparisons in Table 7 cover only the seven easy datasets. Consequently, the evidence supports improved overall compression, but less conclusively establishes superiority over equally trained and adapted alternatives on OOD data.

The lossy extension has a substantive specification ambiguity. Equations 22–24 select k occupancy-code locations and then predict a nonzero code at each location; expanding those codes can produce a number of child points different from k. Thus, the claimed preservation of point count needs a clearer definition of the represented scale and candidate locations. Table 4 also switches to a different, single-stage lossy model, and parameters rise from 9.77M to 14.92M, qualifying the claim that one unchanged model handles both modes.

The originality is primarily in combining and adapting established techniques. Checkerboard context grouping, channel factorization, and parameter-efficient codec adaptation have acknowledged precedents. Theorem 1 formalizes a representational bijection, while Theorem 2 establishes a maximum geometric span rather than equivalent effective information flow under arbitrary sparsity. These arguments motivate the design but do not prove universal robustness or explain the measured gains by themselves.

Several claims exceed the evidence. The 13-dataset best-result statement combines specialized and unified variants; AnyPcc-U alone does not dominate all datasets, and neither variant wins on GS or S3DIS. Seven datasets are omitted from lossy evaluation, and their lossless rankings cannot establish their lossy rate–distortion performance. These limitations narrow the supported scope without negating the strong lossless results.

Deployment and reproducibility claims need greater precision. Section 9.4 calls 2.84 seconds an extreme latency upper bound despite substantially longer per-dataset times in Figure 9, and neither real-time suitability nor standards compatibility is demonstrated. Training splits and hyperparameters are documented well, but exact corruption settings and an accessible code/data link are absent from the supplied manuscript.
